questions.stem: Which file extension identifies a classic Windows command-line batch script?
questions.explanation: Windows batch files use the .bat extension for the classic command line.
questions.trap: .ps1 is PowerShell, .sh is a Linux shell script, and .py is Python - only .bat is the classic Windows batch file.

questions.stem: Which scripting language is used for modern Windows system administration and works with cmdlets to manage the whole OS?
questions.explanation: PowerShell scripts (.ps1) are used for modern Windows administration and use cmdlets to manage the entire OS.
questions.trap: VBScript is for older general Windows/Office automation; the modern admin tool is PowerShell.

questions.stem: Which language, ending in .sh, is used for Linux/Unix shell scripts and is identified by a shebang (#!) at the start of the file?
questions.explanation: Linux/Unix shell scripts end in .sh and start with a shebang (#!) line that identifies the interpreter.
questions.trap: Batch (.bat) and PowerShell (.ps1) are Windows; the .sh shell script with a shebang is the Linux/Unix one.

questions.stem: Which language is described as the king of cross-platform automation that works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, ending in .py?
questions.explanation: Python (.py) is the cross-platform automation choice that runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
questions.trap: JavaScript handles web-browser interactivity; for cross-platform automation scripts the answer is Python.

questions.stem: Which language is used inside web browsers to handle interactivity and ends in .js?
questions.explanation: JavaScript (.js) runs in web browsers to handle interactivity.
questions.trap: Python is cross-platform automation; the browser interactivity language is JavaScript.

questions.stem: Which language is named for general Windows tasks like Office automation and abbreviated VBS?
questions.explanation: Visual Basic Script (VBScript / VBS) is used for general Windows tasks like Office automation.
questions.trap: Bash is Linux/Unix and Python is cross-platform; the Windows/Office automation legacy language is VBScript.

questions.stem: What is the single biggest use case for scripting, per the review?
questions.explanation: The biggest use case is automation - scripts restart machines remotely, update software, remap network drives at login, and run automated backups.
questions.trap: Scripts can touch many areas, but their defining purpose is automating repetitive work, not UI design or encryption.

questions.stem: Why are scripts considered dangerous if mishandled?

choices.text: They cannot be undone once written
They execute commands quickly across many systems, so a mistake spreads fast
They always require a hardware token to run
They only run on a single machine at a time

questions.explanation: Scripts execute commands quickly across many systems, so a mistake spreads fast - a bad script can introduce malware network-wide or crash systems by mishandling resources.
questions.trap: The danger is exactly that scripts scale across many machines at once, not that they're limited to one.

questions.stem: Before deploying a new script across the network, what two precautions does the review recommend?

choices.text: Test it in a sandbox first and have a rollback plan ready
Run it on every machine simultaneously to save time
Disable antivirus so it runs faster
Delete the backups to free space

questions.explanation: Always test scripts in a sandbox before deploying them and have a rollback plan ready in case something goes wrong.
questions.trap: Running untested on every machine at once is precisely the risk; you sandbox-test and keep a rollback path.

questions.stem: A team needs one automation script to run identically on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines. Which language is the best fit?
questions.explanation: Python is the cross-platform choice that runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux from one script.
questions.trap: Batch and VBScript are Windows-only; even PowerShell is rooted in Windows administration. Python is the cross-platform answer.
